stories.headline: Rajnath Singh meets US Secy of War Hegseth on sidelines of ASEAN defence ministers’ meeting in Philippines
stories.title: Rajnath Singh meets US Secy of War Hegseth on sidelines of ASEAN defence ministers’ meeting in Philippines
stories.summary: Philippines, October 28 : Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Wednesday met US War Secretary Pete Hegseth on sidelines of the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu, Philippines. The Defence Minister is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from the United States, Japan, Australia and from other participating nations. The US War Secretary said during the meeting, the counterparts "celebrated the one-year anniversary of the Framework for our Major Defense Partnership and explored ways to strengthen cooperation." In a post on X, Pete Hegseth said, "Great meeting with Indian Minister of Defence Singh. We celebrated the one-year anniversary of the Framework for our Major Defense Partnership and explored ways to strengthen cooperation." The meeting comes as after the meeting in 2025, both leaders signed the ‘framework for the US-India major defence partnership’. The 2025 framework marked a new chapter to further transform the partnership over the next 10 years. According to the Ministry of Defence, it is intended to provide a unified vision and policy direction to deepen defence cooperation. Meanwhile, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth also met representatives from South Korea, Australia and Japan. For his meeting with South Korean Defence Minister Kang, he said, "Great meeting with ROK Minister of National Defense Kang at ADMM-Plus. The U.S.-ROK Alliance is built on peace through strength—ready forces, decisive capability, and combined lethality that deters aggression. America stands with allies that are serious about their own defense." For his meeting with Australian Deputy Prime Minister Marles, he said," It was a pleasure to meet with Australian Deputy Prime Minister Marles. Together, we are optimizing the Alliance to strengthen deterrence and deliver results." For his meeting with Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, he said, " I met with Japan’s Minister of Defense Shinjirō Koizumi @shinjirokoiz to advance our shared vision of peace through strength. Our strategic alignment is essential to building a credible denial defense—supported by increased investment, greater access, more realistic training, and stronger production of the munitions our forces need." The developments come as Rajnath Singh arrived in Cebu, on Tuesday night to attend the ADMM-Plus, where he will address shared regional and international security issues. Upon his arrival at Cebu airport, Singh received a ceremonial welcome from M Gen Fabian M Pedregosa PAF (Retd), Undersecretary of the Department of National Defence of the Philippines. Indian Ambassador to the Philippines Harsh Kumar Jain and Defence Attaché Captain ChandraKant Kothari were also present to welcome the Defence Minister. Singh later interacted with members of the Indian community and Filipino nationals upon arriving at his hotel. On Thursday, the Defence Minister will represent India at the ADMM-Plus meeting and address the forum on common regional and international security challenges. Before departing for Cebu, Singh reiterated India's commitment to strengthening its engagement with ASEAN and promoting stability across the Indo-Pacific region. In a post on X, he said, “India is firmly committed to ASEAN centrality and the peace, stability, and collective growth of the Indo-Pacific region under our Act East Policy.” On the sidelines of the meeting, Singh is scheduled to hold bilateral discussions with defence counterparts from several participating countries, including the host nation, the Philippines, as well as the United States, Japan, Australia, Singapore, Vietnam and South Korea. (ANI)

article_sentences: Fishermen of this coastal town of Thoothukudi abstained from fishing for the second consecutive day on Tuesday (October 27, 2027) following warning on Cyclone ‘Arnab’.

As the India Meteorological Department had warned that the sea would be rough in the wake of the cyclone in the Bay of Bengal, the boats involved in deep sea fishing have been urged to return to the shore immediately.
Fishermen operating the mechanised boats from Thoothukudi Fishing Harbour did not go venture into the sea on Monday.
They abstained from fishing for the second day on Tuesday as there was no improvement in the weather.
Only a few fishermen from Terespuram and New Harbour Beach ventured into the sea on country boats in areas closer to the shore and returned with small catch.

The New Harbour Beach fishermen tested their fortune with ‘Karai Madi’ (shore net), which is cast in the sea at a distance from the shore from a boat and is retrieved by more than 30 people standing on the shore.
After hours of toiling in dragging the fishnet, the fishermen had to be content with around 350 kg sardines, smaller trevally, and white snapper fishes.

stories.title: Cyclone Arnab: Clear fallen trees within two hours, restore power once winds ease, Naidu tells officials
stories.summary: The Chief Minister holds a teleconference with about 32,000 officials and field staff on Wednesday morning
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has directed officials to accelerate relief and restoration operations in areas affected by Cyclone Arnab and said all departments must work in close coordination to restore normalcy at the earliest.

The Chief Minister held a statewide teleconference on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) morning with around 32,000 personnel, including district Collectors and field-level staff, to assess the cyclone’s impact and review the measures being taken to minimise public inconvenience.
He had reviewed the situation until 1.30 a.m. before convening the early-morning meeting.
During a separate review with senior officials, Mr. Naidu sought details of agricultural losses and directed the authorities to prepare preliminary estimates of crop damage.
He also instructed officials to apprise the Centre of the measures being undertaken by the State government to tackle the cyclone’s impact.
Appreciating officials and field-level personnel for working through the night, the Chief Minister urged them to maintain the same dedication until the situation returned to normal.
According to the information available at the time of the review, no loss of life had been reported.
He attributed the outcome to the advance precautions taken by the administration and said the preventive efforts must be sustained.
Mr. Naidu directed officials to restore essential services and clear road obstructions on a priority basis.
Fallen trees blocking roads must be removed and traffic restored within two hours and obstructions on national highways should be cleared immediately to ensure uninterrupted movement of vehicles.
Electricity supply disrupted in affected areas must be restored as soon as wind conditions subside and it is safe for restoration teams to resume work, he said.
The Chief Minister also asked officials to provide adequate food, drinking water and medical facilities at cyclone relief shelters.

stories.headline: Heavy rain alert for 9 Jharkhand districts amid cyclone Arnab
stories.title: Heavy rain alert for 9 Jharkhand districts amid cyclone Arnab
stories.summary: Ranchi, Oct 28 : Weather conditions have changed across Jharkhand under the influence of the severe cyclonic storm 'Arnab', which originated in the Bay of Bengal. Several parts of the state, including the capital Ranchi, have been witnessing rainfall since Wednesday morning, prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to issue a heavy rainfall warning for nine districts. The IMD has warned of heavy rainfall in Ranchi, Khunti, Simdega, Gumla, Lohardaga, Bokaro, Seraikela-Kharsawan, and East and West Singhbhum districts. The impact of the cyclone is also expected to bring down temperatures across Jharkhand by around three to four degrees Celsius. In view of the prevailing weather conditions and the possibility of further deterioration, authorities have ordered the suspension of classes from kindergarten (KG) to Class 12 in Ranchi and Lohardaga districts on October 28 and 29 as a precautionary measure. In Ranchi, intermittent showers have continued since Wednesday morning, while the sky remains overcast. Rainfall accompanied by strong winds has brought a noticeable change in the weather, with temperatures dropping across the city. Similar conditions have been reported from several other parts of Jharkhand, including Hazaribagh, Koderma, Chaibasa, Deoghar, Giridih and Bokaro, where cloudy skies and rainfall have affected normal weather conditions. Meteorological Department scientist Abhishek Anand explained that Jharkhand's geographical location means the Singhbhum region is likely to experience the cyclone's effects first. Thereafter, rainfall and strong winds may spread to other parts of the state, depending on the storm's movement and intensity. The Meteorological Department has urged residents to remain vigilant, particularly in areas where heavy rainfall is expected. Cyclone 'Arnab' reached the Andhra Pradesh coast early Wednesday morning. According to the department's forecast, the cyclone was expected to cross the coast south of Yanam, between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam. During the landfall period, sustained wind speeds were projected to reach 125–135 kmph, while gusts could touch 150 kmph. Amid the changing weather conditions, Ranchi Deputy Commissioner Manjunath Bhajantri convened a meeting with officials from the departments concerned and issued directions to ensure preparedness and a prompt response to any weather-related emergencies. As part of the precautionary arrangements, the electricity department's control room and the Ranchi Municipal Corporation's rapid response team have been placed on alert. The teams have been instructed to respond immediately to incidents such as power supply disruptions and waterlogging caused by heavy rainfall or strong winds. The Railways has also initiated precautionary measures in anticipation of the cyclone's impact. According to information released by the Railways, the operations of at least half a dozen trains either originating from Jharkhand or passing through the state have been cancelled in view of the prevailing conditions. The administration has appealed to residents to take necessary precautions during thunderstorms and periods of strong winds. Commuters have also been urged to exercise caution while travelling on roads affected by waterlogging and to remain alert to changing conditions. The public has been asked to follow weather warnings issued by the Meteorological Department and comply with instructions from the local administration to minimise the risk of accidents and other emergencies. stories.headline: Andhra reports no casualties after cyclone Arnab, says CM Naidu
stories.title: Andhra reports no casualties after cyclone Arnab, says CM Naidu
stories.summary: Amaravati, Oct 28 : Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu on Wednesday said no loss of life has been reported so far following Cyclone Arnab, crediting advance precautionary measures taken by the administration for preventing casualties. Speaking during a teleconference with 32,000 personnel, including district collectors, the Chief Minister directed officials to minimise property damage and restore normalcy in cyclone-affected areas at the earliest. "No loss of life has been reported so far due to Cyclone Arnab. The advance precautionary measures taken by the administrative machinery helped prevent casualties," said Naidu in an official press release. The CM instructed officials to clear roads blocked by fallen trees within two hours and ensure immediate removal of trees obstructing national highways. Also, he directed them to restore electricity supply in affected areas once strong winds subsided. Naidu stressed the need to provide adequate food, drinking water and medical facilities at cyclone shelters and asked officials to prevent water from entering agricultural fields, protect horticultural crops and take measures to prevent breaches in tanks and canals. The CM asked officials to prepare preliminary estimates of crop damage and keep National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) personnel on standby. Further, the officials were directed to make full use of the Manamitra system to address public grievances in cyclone-affected areas and ensure that complainants were informed about the action taken to resolve their issues. Meanwhile, Kakinada Superintendent of Police (SP) G Bindu Madhav said, "Cyclone Arnab had significantly affected the district, uprooting a few hundred trees and fewer than 100 electric poles. However, no major damage has been reported and rainfall subsided after 1 am." Madhav said people were evacuated to relief camps as a precautionary measure and remained there due to the strong winds and roar of the storm between midnight and 1 am. The Uppada road, running along the coast, has been completely washed away, he said, adding that rainfall was relatively low in the district with gusty winds causing the main impact. Alluri Sitaramaraju district SP Amit Bardar said the Cyclone had limited impact on the district, as of 9 am, with trees and electric poles uprooted and some roads inundated. "No loss of life or major damage to infrastructure, houses or livestock has been reported so far. We are monitoring the situation closely as water levels may rise due to continued rainfall," Bardar told PTI. An old bridge in Tadiguda village of Anantagiri mandal was washed away, isolating a hamlet, said the SP, adding that alternative arrangements were being made and restoration work was underway. The preliminary assessment indicated limited overall impact, though the situation would continue to be monitored as rainfall persisted, he added. Konaseema district SP Rahul Meena said gusty winds reaching up 130 kmph had uprooted trees and electric poles across the district during the Cyclone late on Tuesday night. No casualties or property damage had been reported. Fallen trees and electric poles had blocked roads and disrupted power supply, he said, adding that electricity connections were expected to be restored by within few hours, while major highways would be cleared within two to three hours. "Konaseema is among the worst-affected districts, with winds reaching up to 130 kmph uprooting trees and electric poles, blocking roads and disrupting power supply," the SP told PTI. Clearance of interior roads could take until evening, he said, adding that wind speeds had reduced and the cyclone had moved towards Kakinada after weakening slightly. More than 10,000 people had been evacuated from low-lying areas and shifted to shelters, according to his preliminary information. Around 495 cyclone shelters and temporary relief centres had been set up. No village inundation had been reported and water accumulated due to the storm surge had drained, he said. Two NDRF teams and as many SDRF teams were deployed a day before the cyclone to conduct road clearance and rescue operations in response to emergency calls, he said. Additional Andhra Pradesh Special Police (APSP) platoons had also been deployed for clearance operations and other tasks, he said, adding that personnel from various departments were working continuously to restore normalcy by evening. PTI

stories.headline: Glacial Retreat—Part 2 : Five factors that make Kashmir's glacial lakes prone to outburst floods
stories.title: Glacial Retreat—Part 2 : Five factors that make Kashmir's glacial lakes prone to outburst floods
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 27: As glaciers retreat and new glacial lakes emerge across the Himalayan landscape, a scientific study has developed a risk-assessment framework to identify lakes in the Upper Indus Sub-Basin that may be more susceptible to glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), a potentially devastating hazard capable of sending sudden surges of water, rocks and debris into downstream valleys. The study, published in Discover Geoscience by Suhail Ahmad and co-authors, assessed 775 glacial lakes using a combination of satellite imagery, glacier inventories and terrain modelling to estimate their relative susceptibility to outburst events. Rather than relying on lake size alone, the researchers examined a range of indicators linked to the processes that can trigger a sudden release of water. The assessment comes against the backdrop of substantial changes in the region’s glacial lake landscape. The study mapped 255 lakes covering 34.81 square kilometres in 1990, compared with 775 lakes spread across 37.72 square kilometres in 2025. This represents an increase of 520 lakes and an expansion of approximately 2.91 square kilometres in their combined area. The researchers cautioned, in effect, that the presence of a glacial lake does not automatically mean an outburst is imminent. The danger depends on a combination of physical conditions, including the lake’s connection to glaciers, the terrain surrounding it and the amount of water that can flow into it. To assess these differences, the study used a multi-criteria framework combining the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with a Potential Risk Score Index (PRSI). The method assigns weights to different indicators and combines them into a relative susceptibility score, allowing lakes to be compared according to their potential hazard characteristics. “One of the most important indicators was the susceptibility of surrounding terrain to ice and rock avalanches. Such mass movements can enter a lake, displace water and potentially trigger an outburst,” the study reads. The researchers gave avalanche susceptibility the highest weight in their assessment, reflecting its importance as a recognised triggering mechanism for GLOFs. The study examined steep terrain within each lake’s upstream catchment, particularly slopes exceeding 30 degrees, alongside a critical reach angle of 14 degrees. These measurements were used as proxies for terrain where ice or rock avalanches could potentially reach a lake. “The size of the upstream watershed was assigned the second-highest weight. Larger catchments can channel substantial amounts of water from rainfall, snowmelt and glacier melt into a lake, potentially increasing inflows and pressure on its natural dam,” reads the study. “Lake expansion was another important indicator.” The researchers considered lakes that had expanded by more than 10 per cent, assigning higher susceptibility values to those with greater growth. Newly formed lakes absent from the 1990 inventory were assigned an expansion value of 100 per cent for the assessment. The study notes: “The distance between a lake and the nearest active glacier terminus was also assessed. Lakes within 500 metres of a glacier, particularly those in direct physical contact with it, were treated as more susceptible because of their stronger physical and hydrological connection to the glacier system.” Lake area formed the fifth indicator in the framework. However, the researchers assigned it the lowest relative weight, emphasising that size alone cannot reliably determine whether a lake is likely to burst. While a larger lake may release a greater volume of water if a failure occurs, its susceptibility depends on several interacting factors. “Each indicator was placed into high, moderate or low vulnerability classes, with normalised scores of 1.00, 0.50 and 0.25, respectively. The weighted scores were then combined to calculate the Potential Risk Score Index for all 775 lakes,” the study reads, adding that the “the framework is intended as a preliminary, first-order assessment to help prioritise lakes for further investigation and monitoring. It does not constitute a prediction that a particular lake will burst, nor does it establish the timing or magnitude of a future flood.” The study’s reliance on satellite-derived lake inventories and a 30-metre digital elevation model also means that detailed field investigations remain important. Information on lake depth and water volume, the stability of natural dams and local ground conditions would be needed to refine risk estimates and assess potential consequences for downstream settlements and infrastructure. “For the Himalayan region, where glacial lakes are changing alongside glacier retreat and shifting patterns of snow and ice melt, the findings underline the need to move beyond simply counting lakes. Identifying the lakes with potentially hazardous combinations of terrain, inflow and glacier connectivity could help authorities direct monitoring resources more effectively,” it states. The next step is to translate such assessments into on-ground verification, regular satellite surveillance, early-warning systems where warranted and disaster-response planning for downstream communities. The study offers a screening tool for identifying where attention may be most urgently needed, but its findings must be followed by detailed assessments before individual lakes can be treated as confirmed high-risk threats.

The assessment comes against the backdrop of substantial changes in the region’s glacial lake landscape.
The study mapped 255 lakes covering 34.81 square kilometres in 1990, compared with 775 lakes spread across 37.72 square kilometres in 2025.
This represents an increase of 520 lakes and an expansion of approximately 2.91 square kilometres in their combined area.
The researchers cautioned, in effect, that the presence of a glacial lake does not automatically mean an outburst is imminent.
The danger depends on a combination of physical conditions, including the lake’s connection to glaciers, the terrain surrounding it and the amount of water that can flow into it.
To assess these differences, the study used a multi-criteria framework combining the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with a Potential Risk Score Index (PRSI).
The method assigns weights to different indicators and combines them into a relative susceptibility score, allowing lakes to be compared according to their potential hazard characteristics.
“One of the most important indicators was the susceptibility of surrounding terrain to ice and rock avalanches.
Such mass movements can enter a lake, displace water and potentially trigger an outburst,” the study reads.
The researchers gave avalanche susceptibility the highest weight in their assessment, reflecting its importance as a recognised triggering mechanism for GLOFs.
The study examined steep terrain within each lake’s upstream catchment, particularly slopes exceeding 30 degrees, alongside a critical reach angle of 14 degrees.
These measurements were used as proxies for terrain where ice or rock avalanches could potentially reach a lake.
“The size of the upstream watershed was assigned the second-highest weight.
Larger catchments can channel substantial amounts of water from rainfall, snowmelt and glacier melt into a lake, potentially increasing inflows and pressure on its natural dam,” reads the study.
“Lake expansion was another important indicator.” The researchers considered lakes that had expanded by more than 10 per cent, assigning higher susceptibility values to those with greater growth.
Newly formed lakes absent from the 1990 inventory were assigned an expansion value of 100 per cent for the assessment.
The study notes: “The distance between a lake and the nearest active glacier terminus was also assessed.

Lakes within 500 metres of a glacier, particularly those in direct physical contact with it, were treated as more susceptible because of their stronger physical and hydrological connection to the glacier system.” Lake area formed the fifth indicator in the framework.
However, the researchers assigned it the lowest relative weight, emphasising that size alone cannot reliably determine whether a lake is likely to burst.
While a larger lake may release a greater volume of water if a failure occurs, its susceptibility depends on several interacting factors.
“Each indicator was placed into high, moderate or low vulnerability classes, with normalised scores of 1.00, 0.50 and 0.25, respectively.

The weighted scores were then combined to calculate the Potential Risk Score Index for all 775 lakes,” the study reads, adding that the “the framework is intended as a preliminary, first-order assessment to help prioritise lakes for further investigation and monitoring.

Information on lake depth and water volume, the stability of natural dams and local ground conditions would be needed to refine risk estimates and assess potential consequences for downstream settlements and infrastructure.

The next step is to translate such assessments into on-ground verification, regular satellite surveillance, early-warning systems where warranted and disaster-response planning for downstream communities.

stories.headline: Israel election: exit polls point to no clear winner or majority
stories.title: Israel election: exit polls point to no clear winner or majority
stories.summary: Jerusalem, Oct 28 : Israel's parliamentary election appeared to have produced no clear winner, with exit polls indicating that both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition alliance seeking to replace him had fallen short of the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. According to The Jerusalem Post, the exit polls projected Netanyahu's bloc to secure 51-52 seats, while the opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B'Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu and the Democrats, was expected to win 49-51 seats. Channels 11 and 13 projected both sides to be tied at 51 seats each, while Channel 12's survey gave Netanyahu's bloc a slight edge with 52 seats. The opposition bloc declared victory shortly after the exit poll results were released, although neither side appeared to have a clear route to forming a government. The exit polls also indicated that the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces, could emerge with a slight advantage over Netanyahu's right-wing and far-right coalition in terms of the combined strength of its constituent parties. However, Netanyahu's Likud was projected to remain the single largest party, with around 27 seats, while Yashar was forecast to win 21-22 seats. The results suggested that Netanyahu continued to retain the support of a substantial core of Likud voters despite widespread opposition to his leadership among sections of the Israeli electorate. Nevertheless, the projected seat distribution indicated that his ability to form another coalition government could be constrained by the opposition's combined strength and the potential influence of smaller parties. The election witnessed a historic voter turnout and was described by some as one of the most consequential in Israel's history. It was also marked by record participation among Israeli Arab voters, adding another significant dimension to the electoral contest. Exit polls projected that Israeli Arab parties could collectively secure as many as 18 seats in the Knesset, potentially giving them considerable leverage during the negotiations to form the next government. Their projected strength could make them kingmakers in what is expected to be a prolonged coalition-building process, particularly if Netanyahu's bloc fails to gather the support required to reach the majority threshold, according to The Guardian. With neither camp appearing to have a straightforward path to the required 61 seats, the final distribution of seats and the positions adopted by smaller parties were expected to play a decisive role in determining the next government. Voter turnout in Israel's parliamentary election on Tuesday reached 77.7 per cent of eligible voters by the time polling stations closed at 10 p.m. local time, according to the final update from Israel's Central Elections Committee, which oversees the vote. The turnout was the highest recorded in an Israeli election in 27 years, exceeding the 2022 figure by more than seven percentage points. --IANS

article_sentences: A petitioner challenging the appointments of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi has filed an application in the Supreme Court seeking to produce records obtained under the Right to Information (RTI) Act to allege that the selection committees did not specifically assess whether the appointees had experience in conducting elections or possessed the requisite integrity.
In an application seeking amendment of his writ petition, petitioner.

Suri Payala has contended that records obtained from the Legislative Department show that the material placed before the Search Committee and the Selection Committee consisted primarily of lists of candidates, service particulars, dates and service records.
According to him, the records do not disclose any specific assessment of the candidates' integrity or experience in election management and conduct.

The petitioner has challenged the appointments made in March 2024 and February 2025 under the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.

The petitioner contends that Section 5 of the 2023 Act requires the Search Committee to prepare a panel of five persons eligible for appointment as Election Commissioners, while Section 6 governs the Selection Committee's recommendation.
He argues that the records do not show a specific assessment of whether the candidates possessed experience in the conduct of elections or satisfied the requirement relating to integrity.
According to the application, the minutes of the selection process refer to candidates being considered on the basis of their eligibility and experience.
However, the petitioner alleges that the underlying records do not disclose any specific exercise to ascertain their election-related experience or integrity.
He further contends that merely recording that Section 5 was noted, without disclosing how its requirements were assessed, does not demonstrate compliance with the statutory framework.

With respect to the appointments of Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu as ECs made on March 14, 2024, the petitioner has questioned the process through which the Search Committee shortlisted candidates for two vacancies.
The application states that the agenda contemplated a panel of ten names, but the committee ultimately recommended six candidates.

stories.title: Over 1 lakh voter cases cloud Kolkata civic polls as Opposition questions election timeline
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The State Election Commission has released draft rolls for 209 newly delimited KMC wards, but Opposition parties have questioned the November 12 deadline amid concerns over more than one lakh voter cases.

Kolkata: Nearly 32 lakh voters, 209 newly delimited wards, and more than one lakh disputed voter cases have put Kolkata’s municipal election preparations under scrutiny, with Opposition parties questioning whether the electoral machinery has enough time to resolve discrepancies before it publishes the final rolls.

The State Election Commission has circulated draft electoral rolls and proposed polling-station layouts for all 209 wards of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), setting November 12 as the deadline for filing claims and objections.
However, the release of the draft documents has done little to ease concerns over voter verification, pending tribunal cases and the impact of electoral-roll revisions.
The controversy has also brought election timing into sharper focus.

Opposition parties have sought to postpone the civic polls, arguing that the exercise should not proceed until the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process and the Special Summary Revision announced by the Election Commission of India are complete.

The draft rolls and proposed booth arrangements were presented to political parties at the New Administrative Building in Alipore by senior officials of the South 24-Parganas district administration, led by the additional district magistrate.
The draft electoral rolls cover nearly 32 lakh voters across the 209 wards.

While the publication marks a step towards preparing for the civic elections, Opposition representatives have questioned whether the schedule allows sufficient time to scrutinise the changes and establish the status of voters whose cases remain unresolved.
Their concerns centre on the combined workload arising from ward delimitation, voter-roll revision and the allocation of polling stations.
With November 12 as the deadline, parties argue that officials must verify voter movements, identify discrepancies and address pending appeals within a compressed timeframe.
They have described examining the changes and correcting thousands of discrepancies in just over two weeks as logistically impossible.
